also: to cut a long story short

evidence: Cic. Att. 14.1.1; Off. 1.149 (Lewis & Short, s.v. summa)
terms.comment: Sums up what has been said: “all in all, in a word”. Common in Cicero’s letters and in talk (Petronius’ freedmen).

evidence: Cic. Q. Fr. 2.16.3: in summā quattuor sententiīs (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Of a count: “in all”. In post-Augustan prose also “at last”.
“Altogether, at all”; with numbers “in all, only”. For the adjective (“the overall picture”) use tōtus or ūniversus (see whole).

terms.gloss: in short, basically (what more need I say?)
evidence: Cic. Q. Fr. 2.7.3: quid multa? tenent omnia
Cic. Att. 7.4.3: quid multa? nihil mē aliud cōnsōlātur nisi quod …
terms.comment: The speaker’s “basically”: it cuts a story short and goes to the point. So too quid plūra? and nē multa (Lewis & Short, s.v. multus).
“To gather it into a few (words)”; to someone else, in pauca cōnfer!, make it brief! (Plaut. Poen. 5.4.54, Lewis & Short s.v. paucus).
Traupman’s phrase, of classical words; not found as a phrase in Lewis & Short or the loci.

phrases.latin: ad summam, quotīdiē mē solēbam ad illum mētīrī
phrases.english: in short, I used to measure myself against it every day
All in all, we had a good time.

phrases.latin: ut in pauca cōnferam, testāmentō factō mulier moritur
phrases.english: to put it briefly, the woman makes her will and dies
